samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Gilead Sciences announced on October 16, 2023, its planned participation in the 19th European AIDS Conference (EACS), where it would present new data on long-acting HIV treatment strategies. The conference took place in Warsaw, Poland, from October 18-21, 2023. Presentations included new findings on Gilead's twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir (Sunlenca), a first-in-class, long-acting HIV-1 capsid inhibitor. A key focus was the two-year data from the pivotal Phase 2/3 CAPELLA trial, which evaluated lenacapavir's effectiveness and safety in combination with other antiretrovirals for heavily treatment-experienced adults with multi-drug resistant HIV. The data demonstrated that resistance to lenacapavir was infrequent and primarily occurred in participants with poor adherence to their background drug regimen. Additionally, Gilead presented findings from a survey of healthcare professionals involved in the CAPELLA trial, which indicated positive perceptions of lenacapavir and its potential to improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for this patient population. <2> Gilead Sciences announced on October 3, 2023, that it would present new data from its virology research programs at the IDWeek 2023 conference, held in Boston from October 11-15. The presentations included long-term, real-world efficacy and safety data on its HIV treatment Biktarvy from the observational BICSTaR study. The company also presented two-year data from the pivotal CAPELLA trial, which evaluated the long-acting injectable lenacapavir (Sunlenca) for heavily treatment-experienced adults with multi-drug resistant HIV; these results were presented at the 19th European AIDS Conference (EACS 2023) from October 18-21 in Warsaw, Poland, rather than at IDWeek. The CAPELLA data showed that resistance to lenacapavir was infrequent and primarily occurred in participants with poor adherence or a lack of fully active antiretrovirals in their background regimen. <3> On September 5, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted tentative approval to Viatris Inc. for a new pediatric formulation to treat HIV-1. [1, 3, 6] The drug is a fixed-dose combination of abacavir 60 mg, dolutegravir 5 mg, and lamivudine 30 mg, designed as strawberry-flavored tablets for oral suspension. [1, 6] This once-daily treatment is indicated for children weighing at least 6 kg. [1, 5] The approval was granted through the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) program, signifying that the formulation meets the FDA's standards for quality, safety, and efficacy. [1] The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends this drug combination as a preferred first-line regimen for children with HIV. [2, 3] This development is crucial as it helps address the significant gap in treatment coverage for children living with HIV, aiming to reduce pill burden and improve adherence. [1, 3] <4> GLAAD, in collaboration with the Gilead COMPASS Initiative®, published its fourth annual State of HIV Stigma Study, which surveyed 2,533 U.S. adults in February 2023. The report, released on August 25, 2023, reveals a concerning knowledge gap regarding HIV among Gen Z when compared to older generations like Gen X. Despite this, the study also indicates sustained progress in public awareness that medications can be used for HIV prevention and to treat the virus to the point of being undetectable and untransmittable (U=U). <5> The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) hosted the sixth biennial 'Strategies for an HIV Cure' meeting in Bethesda, MD, on October 12-13, 2023. [1, 3] The primary purpose of the meeting was to review research progress by those funded through the NIH Martin Delaney Collaboratories (MDCs) for HIV Cure Research program. [1, 2] The event aimed to foster communication and collaboration among the ten MDCs and to gather feedback from their Scientific and Community Advisory Boards. [1] The two-day, in-person meeting, which was open to the public at no cost, featured presentations from the ten collaboratories and two Centers for Innovative HIV/AIDS Vaccine and Cure Research (CIAVCR), and also included poster sessions. [1, 2] A livestream of the proceedings was made available and archived for later viewing. [1] <6> On July 28, 2023, the Janssen Pharmaceutical Companies of Johnson & Johnson announced the submission of a supplemental New Drug Application (sNDA) to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The application seeks to expand the indication for their HIV-1 therapy, EDURANT® (rilpivirine), to include treatment for children weighing 10 kilograms or more. This submission, supported by data from the Phase 2 PAINT and PICTURE studies, aims to provide a new treatment option for younger pediatric patients. In parallel, a similar application was submitted to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for expanded pediatric use in Europe. <7> The 12th International AIDS Society (IAS) Conference on HIV Science, designated as IAS 2023, was held in Brisbane, Australia, and virtually from July 23 to 26, 2023. The conference featured significant advancements in HIV research. One key study presented was an open-label extension of the HPTN 084 trial, which revealed that nearly 80% of cisgender women across seven African nations preferred long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) for PrEP over daily oral pills. The research, involving almost 2,500 participants in Botswana, Eswatini, Kenya, Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, found that factors such as being sexually active without a live-in partner and experiences with intimate partner violence influenced this choice. Additionally, the conference addressed the impacts of other infectious diseases on individuals with HIV. A World Health Organization (WHO) analysis of global surveillance data from 2022 indicated that people living with HIV who contracted mpox were not at a higher risk of hospitalization unless they were immunosuppressed with a low CD4 count. Another WHO analysis discussed the mortality risk from COVID-19 among people with HIV, noting it did not decline as significantly during the Omicron wave compared to the general population, emphasizing the need for booster vaccine doses. These findings were highlighted in press conferences and reports associated with the event. <8> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted Fast Track designation to EBT-101, a first-in-class gene-editing therapy that utilizes CRISPR technology. [1] This therapy is currently under investigation as a potential functional cure for HIV-1. [1] The Fast Track designation is a process designed to facilitate the development and expedite the review of drugs that aim to treat serious conditions and address unmet medical needs. [1] <9> A man from Geneva, who has been living with HIV since 1990, is considered the sixth person to be in long-term remission from the virus after receiving a stem cell transplant in July 2018 to treat an aggressive form of leukemia. What makes the "Geneva patient's" case unique and particularly significant to researchers is that unlike the previous five individuals who were cured, the stem cell donor did not have the rare CCR5-delta-32 genetic mutation that blocks HIV from entering cells. The man stopped antiretroviral therapy in November 2021, and more than 20 months later, no detectable virus has been found in his system. While scientists are optimistic, they remain cautious about declaring him "cured," preferring the term "long-term remission" as there is still a possibility the virus could return. Researchers speculate that the transplant itself may have eliminated all infected cells, or that the immunosuppressive drugs he received post-transplant played a role in the outcome. This case opens new avenues for HIV cure research, suggesting that achieving remission may be possible without the CCR5-delta-32 mutation, which could broaden the pool of potential stem cell donors.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On February 5, 2024, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its fact sheet concerning HIV and children, revealing a significant reduction in perinatal HIV transmissions within the United States. Perinatal transmission is noted as the most prevalent method of infection for children under 13 in the U.S. The updated data indicates that 53 cases of HIV were diagnosed in children younger than 13 in the United States and six dependent areas during 2021. This marks a decrease of more than half from the 105 cases that were reported in this demographic in 2017. <2> National Black HIV/AIDS Awareness Day (NBHAAD) is officially observed annually on February 7. First held in 1999, the day aims to increase education, testing, treatment, and community involvement to address the disproportionate impact of HIV on Black communities. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), through platforms like HIV.gov, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) are key federal bodies that recognize and provide resources for the observance. They work alongside numerous community-based organizations to highlight how factors like racism, discrimination, and mistrust in the healthcare system can create barriers to care and prevention for Black Americans. Data from the CDC shows that while progress has been made in reducing new HIV infections among Black people, they still accounted for 40% of new diagnoses in 2021 despite representing only 14% of the U.S. population. The theme for the 2024 observance was “Engage, Educate, Empower: Uniting to End HIV/AIDS in Black Communities.” <3> The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) have formally withdrawn their appeal of a significant federal court decision impacting copay accumulator adjustment programs. The action, officially stipulated on January 16, 2024, concludes the government's challenge to a September 2023 ruling by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. That ruling had invalidated a 2021 HHS rule, deeming it "arbitrary and capricious." The 2021 rule had given health insurance plans and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) the discretion to implement copay accumulator programs, which prevent financial assistance from drug manufacturers from counting towards a patient's deductible and annual out-of-pocket maximum. With the appeal dropped, a prior 2020 rule is now in effect. This 2020 rule generally requires that manufacturer copay assistance must be applied to a patient's cost-sharing obligations, but it includes an exception: accumulator programs can still be used for brand-name drugs that have a medically appropriate generic equivalent available. While patient advocacy groups, such as the HIV+Hepatitis Policy Institute who were plaintiffs in the case, praised the withdrawal, HHS has indicated it does not intend to take enforcement action against health plans while it engages in new rulemaking to address the court's decision. <4> A study published on aidsmap.com on December 19, 2023, investigated resistance to the widely used HIV medication dolutegravir. The research analyzed 599 individuals for whom the treatment was failing and found that 36 people, or 6%, had developed some level of resistance to the drug. The study identified that resistance was more likely in individuals taking dolutegravir as a monotherapy or in a dual therapy regimen with lamivudine. Despite these findings, the article notes that treatment failure on dolutegravir occurs in less than 5% of users, and resistance is very unusual when it is part of a combination of three fully active drugs. <5> Effective December 2, 2023, the Armed Services Blood Program (ASBP) implemented new blood donor eligibility guidelines as recommended by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). [1] This update moves away from a time-based deferral for men who have sex with men (MSM) to an individualized risk-based assessment for all donors, regardless of sexual orientation or gender. [1, 2] The new screening procedures eliminate questions specific to MSM. [1, 5] Instead, all potential donors are asked the same questions about their individual HIV risk factors. [1, 5] The updated guidelines introduce a three-month deferral for anyone who has had a new sexual partner or high-risk sexual activity within the last three months. [1, 3] Additionally, new deferral periods are in place for individuals using HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP): a three-month deferral from the last dose of an oral PrEP medication and a two-year deferral from the last dose of an injectable PrEP medication. [1, 2] <6> The White House Office of National AIDS Policy (ONAP) released the National HIV/AIDS Strategy 2023 Interim Action Report on December 1, 2023, to coincide with World AIDS Day. The report details the progress made by the federal government during fiscal years 2022 and 2023 toward the goals of the National HIV/AIDS Strategy (2022-2025). This broader strategy serves as a roadmap to accelerate national efforts to end the HIV epidemic in the United States by 2030. While the report indicates progress toward these goals, it also emphasizes that significant work remains and serves as a continued call to action for all stakeholders. <7> On World AIDS Day, December 1, 2023, the White House Office of National AIDS Policy (ONAP) released the National HIV/AIDS Strategy (NHAS) 2023 Interim Action Report. The report details the progress federal agencies have made during fiscal years 2022 and 2023 toward the goals of the broader National HIV/AIDS Strategy for 2022-2025. This national strategy, originally released in December 2021, provides a roadmap to reduce new HIV infections by 75% by 2025 and end the HIV epidemic in the U.S. by 2030. The interim report indicates that while progress is being made, continued and accelerated efforts are necessary to achieve the strategy's objectives. <8> On November 30, 2023, President Joe Biden issued a formal proclamation designating December 1, 2023, as World AIDS Day, marking the 35th observance of the event. [1] In the proclamation, the President highlighted the significant progress made in treating and preventing HIV while acknowledging that approximately 39 million people worldwide, including over one million in the United States, are still living with the virus. [1] The announcement detailed the administration's commitment to ending the HIV/AIDS epidemic by 2030 through a dual approach: the National HIV/AIDS Strategy for the U.S. and the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) for the global community. [1, 2] Key initiatives mentioned include a request for $850 million for the Ending the HIV Epidemic Initiative, efforts to reform HIV criminalization laws, and a commitment to secure a clean, five-year reauthorization of the life-saving PEPFAR program. [1, 2] <9> The U.S. Business Action to End HIV coalition convened its annual meeting in Washington, D.C. on November 30, 2023, bringing together nearly 60 business leaders to discuss private sector advancements in combating the HIV epidemic. [1] The meeting served as a platform to review the coalition's impact in 2023 and outline priorities for 2024. [1] Esteemed speakers included White House Director of National AIDS Policy Harold Phillips and CDC Acting Director of HIV Prevention Dr. Robyn Neblett-Fanfair. [1] Following the meeting, a reception was held to honor World AIDS Day, which featured a keynote address by Dr. Anthony Fauci. [1] The events aimed to foster collaboration among private sector entities, policymakers, and healthcare advocates to accelerate progress toward ending HIV in the United States. [3] <10> Gilead Sciences announced on October 16, 2023, its planned participation in the 19th European AIDS Conference (EACS), where it would present new data on long-acting HIV treatment strategies. The conference took place in Warsaw, Poland, from October 18-21, 2023. Presentations included new findings on Gilead's twice-yearly injectable lenacapavir (Sunlenca), a first-in-class, long-acting HIV-1 capsid inhibitor. A key focus was the two-year data from the pivotal Phase 2/3 CAPELLA trial, which evaluated lenacapavir's effectiveness and safety in combination with other antiretrovirals for heavily treatment-experienced adults with multi-drug resistant HIV. The data demonstrated that resistance to lenacapavir was infrequent and primarily occurred in participants with poor adherence to their background drug regimen. Additionally, Gilead presented findings from a survey of healthcare professionals involved in the CAPELLA trial, which indicated positive perceptions of lenacapavir and its potential to improve clinical outcomes and quality of life for this patient population.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In March 2025, North Dakota became the fourth state in the U.S. and the first in the Midwest to fully repeal its law criminalizing HIV exposure. [3, 4] Governor Kelly Armstrong signed the bipartisan House Bill 1217 into law, a measure that repeals North Dakota Century Code § 12.1-20-17. [1, 3, 8] The previous law, enacted during the height of the HIV epidemic, made it a Class A felony for a person with HIV to willfully transfer bodily fluids, regardless of intent to transmit or if transmission occurred. [1, 2, 4] Supported by the ACLU of North Dakota, Shine Bright & Live, and the Department of Health and Human Services, the repeal is recognized as a significant step toward aligning state law with modern science, which shows that individuals on effective treatment cannot transmit the virus. [1, 3, 4] Advocates believe that decriminalizing HIV will reduce stigma, encourage testing and treatment, and better protect the constitutional rights of individuals living with the health condition. [1, 3, 4] <2> AIDSWatch, the largest and oldest constituent-led HIV federal advocacy event in the United States, will be held in Washington, D.C. from March 31 to April 2, 2025. Organized by AIDS United, the event is expected to bring together over 500 advocates from across the country to conduct more than 200 meetings with congressional offices. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Health Action Alliance released its 'U.S. Business Action to End HIV: August 2025 Action Report' on August 28, 2025. The report details recent developments concerning HIV in the United States, including information about a new $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program that could serve as a source of funding for HIV/AIDS services. The report also highlights CVS Health's decision not to add Gilead's new twice-yearly HIV prevention drug, Yeztugo, to its commercial and Affordable Care Act (ACA) formularies. CVS Health cited clinical, financial, and regulatory factors for its decision regarding the drug, which has a list price of over $28,000 a year. <2> Dr. Ted Cory, an associate professor at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center (UTHSC) College of Pharmacy, has been awarded a $154,000 grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH). The grant will fund research aimed at improving the delivery of antiretroviral drugs to hidden HIV reservoirs within the body, such as macrophage cells. This research, conducted with co-investigator Professor Santosh Kumar, PhD, seeks to enhance the effectiveness of current HIV therapies by investigating how to improve drug penetration into these cells where the virus can hide. Ultimately, the project represents a significant step toward the goal of complete viral eradication. <3> Reports emerged that the Trump administration was withholding funds.; The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) was involved.; More than half of $6 billion was being withheld. <4> The Wistar Institute has been awarded a five-year, $17 million grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to establish the iCure Consortium, an initiative aimed at developing personalized HIV cure regimens. The consortium will research a multi-faceted approach that combines several advanced techniques tailored to each patient's specific HIV strain. These strategies include using neutralizing antibodies, engineered CAR-T and natural killer (NK) cells to destroy infected cells, and precision latency-reversing drugs designed to awaken dormant HIV, making it vulnerable to the immune system. <5> The Health Action Alliance's 'July 2025 Action Report' detailed a meeting that took place on July 16, 2025, in Washington, D.C.. A delegation of business leaders from the U.S. Business Action to End HIV met with the Office of Management and Budget and the office of Senator Tim Scott (R-SC). The delegation included representatives from Alchemy, Avita Care Solutions, Gilead, MISTR, Molecular Testing Labs, and ViiV Healthcare. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the coalition's dedication to national efforts to end HIV and to stress the importance of continued investment in funding for HIV prevention and treatment. <6> The #SaveHIVFunding campaign, in partnership with organizations including AIDS United, Families USA, and Popular Democracy, launched 'Accountability August' to advocate for robust Fiscal Year 2026 funding for federal HIV programs. The initiative aims to hold elected officials accountable for their votes on HIV funding by organizing in-district meetings during the congressional recess. It specifically highlights the devastating impact of potential funding cuts on vulnerable communities, particularly in battleground states with a high HIV burden and weakened public health infrastructures. The campaign provides an advocacy toolkit with social media assets and call scripts to urge Congress to reject cuts and fully fund these life-saving programs. <7> On July 25, 2025, the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) announced it had adopted a positive opinion for Gilead's HIV prevention drug, lenacapavir. The decision occurred during the CHMP meeting held from July 21-24, 2025. In addition to the recommendation for use as a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in the EU, the CHMP also issued a favorable EU-Medicines for all (EU-M4all) opinion. This specific opinion is designed to streamline the assessment for World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification and to facilitate faster national regulatory evaluations in low- and lower-middle-income countries. <8> American Gene Technologies (AGT), a U.S. clinical-stage biotechnology company, announced compelling new data from its AGT103-T HIV cure program in a late-breaker oral presentation at the 13th International AIDS Society Conference on HIV Science (IAS 2025) in Kigali, Rwanda. [7, 8, 9] The presentation detailed findings from the Phase 1 trial where all five evaluable patients showed a significant reduction in the Intact Proviral HIV DNA reservoir following treatment with the cell and gene therapy. [7, 8] Notably, one participant's HIV reservoir became undetectable by Day 500, a suppression that was sustained for over two years. [8, 9] AGT reported these results underscore the therapy's potential to reduce the replication-competent HIV reservoir, a critical step towards a functional cure. [8] The company plans to start larger trials in 2026 to further validate the findings. [9] <9> Research presented at the 13th International AIDS Society Conference on HIV Science (IAS 2025) in Kigali, Rwanda, shows that recent cuts in U.S. funding for HIV programs have led to immediate decreases in HIV testing and treatment initiations in several countries. [1] A study by Anova Health, comparing the first quarter of 2024 with the first quarter of 2025, revealed an 8.5% reduction in testing, a 31% drop in HIV diagnoses, and a 30% decrease in treatment initiations. [1] The conference was held from July 13 to July 17, 2025. [2, 3, 4, 8] <10> On July 17, 2025, the Democratic Staff of the Committee on Oversight and Accountability, led by Ranking Member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) and joined by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), sent a letter to the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The letter expressed grave concern over what it described as the "systematic" disruption and elimination of federal funding for HIV prevention, treatment, and research under the Trump Administration. The lawmakers requested documents and information regarding these funding cuts, questioning whether the motivations were based on sound science or misinformation. The letter highlighted specific actions, such as the elimination of the HIV prevention division at the CDC, and warned that these cuts could reverse decades of progress and cost lives.
